title: 2 Chronicles 3:1–7
context: Solomon begins to build the LORD’s house in Jerusalem “on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David his father,” on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, in the second day of the second month of the fourth year of his reign. The site notice is unique in this form. Genesis 22 places Abraham’s offering in the land of Moriah, on one of the mountains there; this verse names the temple site Mount Moriah and ties it to the LORD’s appearing to David. 2 Samuel 24 and 1 Chronicles 21 tell of the threshing floor, called Araunah’s in Samuel and Ornan’s in Chronicles, and those notes already connect the place with the later temple. The links are shared ground, or at least to be held with a light hand: the Chronicler names Moriah and David’s threshing floor together; Genesis 22 is not retold here, and the two personal names for the Jebusite should be reported, not forced into one spelling. The date agrees with 1 Kings 6:1 on the fourth year and the second month, though that verse also names the month Ziv and counts four hundred and eighty years after the exodus, a notice this verse does not include. Other measurements that differ from 1 Kings 6 are named in the verse notes rather than listed in full here. Both traditions keep the measurements as building report, refuse allegory, and invent no party contrast over the site or the numbers.

verses.text: Then Solomon began to build the LORD’s house at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David his father, which he prepared in the place that David had appointed, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon begins to build “the LORD’s house at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David his father,” in the place David had appointed, “on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.” Genesis 22 locates Abraham’s offering in the land of Moriah; this verse uses the name Mount Moriah for the temple site and joins it to the LORD’s appearing to David. 2 Samuel 24 calls the owner Araunah the Jebusite; 1 Chronicles 21, like this verse, uses Ornan. The already drafted notes on those chapters already point ahead to this site as the later house, and they leave the silver and gold figures of the purchase unresolved. The connections are to be named as shared or carefully hedged, not as a contrast and not as a typological system the verse does not spell out.

Arminian readers take the Chronicler’s site notice as the text gives it: Moriah, the appearance to David, and Ornan’s floor, held beside Genesis 22 and the two census stories without forcing one narrative.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also refuse a party fork here. The place-name Moriah, the appearance to David, and the threshing floor are the Chronicler’s own links; Genesis 22, 2 Samuel 24, and 1 Chronicles 21 stand as the related texts already drafted, with Araunah and Ornan both reported.

Both traditions keep the identification modest and shared, and they do not turn Isaac’s offering or David’s altar into an allegory of the temple’s later rooms.

verses.text: He began to build in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He began to build in the second day of the second month, in the fourth year of his reign.” 1 Kings 6:1 also places the start in the fourth year, in the month Ziv, which is the second month, and adds a count of four hundred and eighty years after Israel came out of Egypt. This verse gives a day, the second of the month, and does not include that larger date. The already drafted 1 Kings 6 notes treat the four hundred and eighty years as that book’s dating notice.

Arminian readers keep both dates in view: the second day is named here, Ziv and the long count there, without filling this verse from the other book.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stay consistent with those Kings notes. The fourth year and the second month agree; the exodus count of 1 Kings 6:1 is not restated here, and the second day is this verse’s own detail.

Both traditions leave the two notices unmerged and invent no contrast over the missing years.

verses.text: Now these are the foundations which Solomon laid for the building of God’s house: the length by cubits after the first measure was sixty cubits, and the width twenty cubits.
verses.arminianNotes:
The foundations of God’s house are given “by cubits after the first measure”: “sixty cubits, and the width twenty cubits.” 1 Kings 6:2 has the same length and width, “a length of sixty cubits, and its width twenty,” and adds “its height thirty cubits”, a figure this verse does not supply. The cubit is a common ancient measure, from the elbow to the fingertip, often taken as about eighteen inches; no more exact modern conversion is pressed, and the numbers are not treated as a code.

Arminian readers take the sixty by twenty as a building measure, matching 1 Kings 6:2 in plan, without reading a doctrine out of the missing height.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the agreement and the silence. Length and width match; the height of thirty cubits stands in 1 Kings 6:2 and not here.

Both traditions refuse to allegorize the foundations or to invent a reason for the omitted height.

verses.text: The porch that was in front, its length, across the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and the height one hundred twenty; and he overlaid it within with pure gold.
verses.arminianNotes:
The porch in front has a length of twenty cubits, “and the height one hundred twenty”; and he overlaid it within with pure gold. 1 Kings 6:3 gives a porch length of twenty cubits along the width of the house, and a width, or depth, of ten cubits, and does not state a height of one hundred twenty. The two descriptions should be reported as they stand. The extraordinary height has been discussed in many ways; no solution the text does not give is chosen, and the number is not turned into a symbol.

Arminian readers keep the twenty-cubit length as shared and leave the height of one hundred twenty unharmonized with 1 Kings 6:3.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers do the same. The porch length agrees; the height named here is not in 1 Kings 6:3, which instead gives a depth of ten cubits.

Both traditions stay with a descriptive reading and refuse allegory or a forced textual theory.

verses.text: He made the larger room with a ceiling of cypress wood, which he overlaid with fine gold, and ornamented it with palm trees and chains.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He made the larger room with a ceiling of cypress wood, which he overlaid with fine gold, and ornamented it with palm trees and chains.” The greater hall is described in materials and ornament, cypress, gold, palms, and chains, as a built room, not as a figure of something else. 1 Kings 6 describes cedar lining, carvings, and gold in related but not identical terms.

Arminian readers take the overlay and the ornaments as the house’s actual finish, reported without a hidden sense in the palms or the chains.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the verse in the register of construction. The larger room, its cypress ceiling, and its gold and carved work are to be read as they are written.

Both traditions name the 1 Kings 6 parallel without merging the wording or allegorizing the decoration.

verses.text: He decorated the house with precious stones for beauty. The gold was gold from Parvaim.
verses.arminianNotes:
He decorated the house with precious stones for beauty. “The gold was gold from Parvaim.” The stones are said to be for beauty, a purpose the verse itself names. Parvaim is given as the source of the gold; its location is not identified here, and no certain site should be claimed.

Arminian readers leave Parvaim modestly unexplained and refuse to turn the precious stones into a moral or mystical code.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take “for beauty” as the stated reason and treat Parvaim as a place-name whose exact site remains uncertain.

Both traditions keep the verse as a description of costly finish, not as an allegory of later worship.

verses.text: He also overlaid the house, the beams, the thresholds, its walls, and its doors with gold, and engraved cherubim on the walls.
verses.arminianNotes:
He overlaid “the house, the beams, the thresholds, its walls, and its doors with gold, and engraved cherubim on the walls.” Gold covers the structure, and cherubim are cut into the walls, as in the related work of 1 Kings 6, though the wording is not the same. The engraving is part of the house’s decoration, not a puzzle to be solved into a system.

Arminian readers hear a thorough overlay and carved cherubim, the house made ready as a holy place, without pressing the gold into a symbol of something the verse does not name.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also stay descriptive. Beams, thresholds, walls, and doors are overlaid, and cherubim are engraved, a report to be set beside 1 Kings 6 and not rewritten from it.

Both traditions close the unit still refusing to allegorize the measurements or the gold.
